learning_outcomes.description: understand the nature and significance of poetry
recognise and discuss a poem's stylistic features
utilise skills in the craft of poetry writing
edit your poetry and provide feedback to other writers
understand principles and trends in the business of writing and publishing

assessments.task_description:
In the first half of semester, you will undertake five guided poetry experiments arising from material introduced in lectures, begun in tutorials and developed through independent revision. They are designed to develop your understanding of image, line, sound, pattern and poetic form.

Your submission will contain work from all five experiments:

  • one haiku
  • one list poem
  • one blues poem
  • one sonnet
  • one free-verse object poem.


For two poems of your choice, include one earlier draft of each. The development from draft to finished poem should demonstrate purposeful revision. The drafts provide evidence of your creative process and are not assessed as additional finished poems.

The portfolio will be assessed on:

  • Response to the experiments: purposeful and imaginative use of the relevant forms and techniques;
  • Poetic craft: precision, freshness and control of language, image, sound, syntax and line;
  • Development and revision: purposeful and substantial development across the portfolio, with specific evidence from the two poems for which earlier versions are submitted.
  • Editing and presentation: careful editing and professional presentation. 


Each poem should begin on a new page. The haiku need not have a title; all other poems should be titled. Place each earlier draft immediately after the finished poem to which it relates and label it clearly “Earlier draft”.

The aim is not to arrive at a finished poem on the first attempt. You are encouraged to try different possibilities, take creative risks and use drafting, discussion and revision to discover what each poem can become.

Use of generative AI: Generative AI must not be used to generate, rewrite or edit any poem, draft, reflection, workshop feedback or writer’s statement submitted for assessment in this course. Standard spelling and grammar checking that does not generate or rewrite text is permitted. You must not upload another student’s poem, feedback or other course material to a generative AI system. If you are uncertain whether a particular tool or use is permitted, consult the Course Coordinator before using it.
assessments.submission_guidelines: Submit your Poetry Experiments Portfolio through Turnitin in Blackboard as a single PDF.
assessments.deferral_or_extension: You may be able to apply for an extension.
assessments.late_submission: A penalty of 10% of the maximum possible mark will be deducted per 24 hours from time submission is due for up to 7 days. After 7 days, you will receive a mark of 0.
assessments.additional_info: You may be able to apply for an extension.

assessments.assessment_title: Poem by Heart: Recitation and Close Reading
assessments.task_description:
Learning a poem by heart allows you to encounter it from the inside: to become attentive to its language, sounds, rhythms, movements and patterns. Memorisation is therefore not simply a test of recall. This task assesses both your attentive recitation and what memorising the poem has helped you understand about how it works.

You will choose a poem from an approved list published on Blackboard. The poems have been selected to provide broadly comparable levels of length and difficulty.

You will complete the assessment individually with your tutor in a ten-minute, in-person appointment. You will:

  • recite the poem from memory;
  • reflect briefly on one thing you noticed or came to understand through memorising it; and
  • take part in a short close-reading conversation with your tutor about the poem’s language, form and poetic techniques.

After the recitation, you will be given a clean copy of the poem to use during the discussion. Your tutor will ask one or two questions that invite you to examine particular words, sounds, images, lines or formal choices. The discussion will focus on close reading and poetic craft rather than biographical or historical knowledge.

The assessment will be marked on:

  • an attentive and substantially accurate recitation;
  • a specific and perceptive reflection on what the process of memorisation revealed;
  • close analysis of the poem’s language, form and poetic techniques; and
  • thoughtful and responsive engagement with the tutor’s questions.

You may sit or stand for the recitation. Minor slips will not substantially affect your mark, and your tutor may provide up to two prompts. Theatrical performance is neither required nor assessed: the emphasis is on knowing the poem attentively, rather than performing it dramatically.

Recording of Oral and Practical Assessment  

  • All presentations will be recorded for marking purposes via recording facilities available where the assessment takes place (eg. ECHO360, Zoom, camera device)  
  • Recordings will be retained by the School of Communication and Arts for at least 12 months from the release of the final grade for the course.  
  • Recordings will be stored in a secure manner and will only be accessed by authorised school staff for the purposes of: 
  • Moderation of marking;  
  • Provision of feedback to the student(s) recorded; and/or  
  • Re-marking following a successful re-mark application.
assessments.submission_guidelines: This assessment will be completed in person during an individually scheduled ten-minute appointment with your tutor. Booking instructions and available appointment times will be provided through Blackboard. Your booked appointment is your assessment due date and time. No electronic submission is required.
assessments.deferral_or_extension: You cannot defer or apply for an extension for this assessment.
assessments.late_submission: A penalty of 10% of the maximum possible mark will be deducted per 24 hours from time submission is due for up to 7 days. After 7 days, you will receive a mark of 0.
assessments.additional_info: You cannot defer or apply for an extension for this assessment.

assessments.task_description:
Workshopping is an essential part of creative practice. This assessment is based on the workshop practice you demonstrate during the six Poetry Workshops in Weeks 8–13.

Across these workshops, you will discuss other students’ poems and have up to three of your own poems workshopped. Your contribution may be demonstrated through spoken discussion and written feedback to other students' poems.

Tutors will consider:

  • Close reading: attentive and perceptive engagement with other students’ poems;
  • Constructive feedback: specific, useful and respectful comments on poetic choices and possibilities;
  • Collaborative discussion: thoughtful contributions that develop the group’s understanding of the poems; and
  • Engagement with feedback: considered reflection on feedback received when your own poems are workshopped.

These aspects will be considered holistically and will not be marked separately. Engagement with feedback applies when your own poem is being workshopped.

Each workshop will be marked out of 2:

  • 2 marks: specific, constructive and perceptive workshop practice demonstrating close engagement with the poems and discussion and, where applicable, thoughtful engagement with feedback;
  • 1 mark: relevant workshop practice demonstrating adequate engagement; or
  • 0 marks: insufficient evidence of workshop practice.


If you miss a workshop, you should, where practicable, return your written feedback on the scheduled poems to your tutor at the next Poetry Workshop. If your own poem was scheduled, it will normally still be discussed and the feedback collected for you. If approved circumstances prevent you from participating in at least five workshops, an equivalent supervised assessment will be arranged.
assessments.submission_guidelines: Workshop Practice is completed during your scheduled Poetry Workshops in Weeks 8–13 and assessed by your tutor in class. No separate submission is required.

assessments.task_description:
Develop and submit a portfolio of five finished poems, accompanied by a writer’s statement of approximately 750 words. The portfolio should represent your strongest work and demonstrate sustained attention to poetic craft, thoughtful revision and your developing voice as a poet. The poems may be connected by subject, voice or form, but they need not constitute a sequence.

At least three poems must be new to this assessment: they must not have appeared in the Poetry Experiments portfolio. You may include substantially reworked versions of up to two poems from that portfolio. These versions must demonstrate significant further development in their conception, language, form or structure; correction or light polishing is not sufficient.

Your portfolio must also include a writer’s statement of approximately 750 words. The statement should reflect thoughtfully on the creative practice and decisions shaping your portfolio. You may write in the first person. Although this is not a conventional research essay, your discussion should refer specifically and accurately to poems, poets and publications. The statement should:

  • explain the principal creative and formal decisions shaping the portfolio;
  • discuss the development and revision of particular poems, using specific examples from earlier and final versions;
  • discuss how at least two poets studied in the course influenced, challenged or helped you understand your own practice, referring to particular poems or techniques;
  • explain how any poem carried forward from the Poetry Experiments Portfolio has been substantially transformed; and
  • identify one contemporary publication outlet suitable for one or more poems in the portfolio, explaining your choice with reference to its editorial interests, readership or recent publications. You should identify which of your poems you would submit and explain why it belongs there.


The assessment will be marked on:

  • Poetic craft: precise, imaginative and purposeful use of language, form and poetic techniques;
  • Creative achievement: the originality, ambition and effectiveness of the poems, individually and as a portfolio;
  • Development and revision: purposeful and substantial development across the portfolio, with specific evidence from the two poems for which earlier versions are submitted; and
  • Writer’s statement: a specific and perceptive account of creative decisions, revision, engagement with poets studied in the course, and publication context.


Each poem should begin on a new page. Place the writer’s statement after the poems. After the statement, include an earlier version of two of the poems discussed in it. These may be new poems developed through workshops or poems carried forward from Poetry Experiments. For each carried-forward poem, include the version submitted for Poetry Experiments. Clearly label all earlier versions. They provide evidence of your creative process and are not assessed as additional finished poems.

The strongest portfolios will not simply display five competent poems. They will show a poet making deliberate and increasingly adventurous decisions — and using revision to discover possibilities that were not present in the first draft.
assessments.submission_guidelines: Submit your Poetry Portfolio and Writer’s Statement through Turnitin in Blackboard as a single PDF. Arrange the submission in this order: five poems, each beginning on a new page; the writer’s statement; and clearly labelled earlier versions of two poems.

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 1 Lecture – Poetry: What even is it?

What makes a poem a poem — and how do we know? We begin by comparing several very different poems and testing some of our assumptions about what poetry looks like, how it sounds and what it can do. The lecture will also introduce the course and its assessments.


Learning outcomes: L01, L02

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 1 Tutorial – Where does a poem begin?

After asking what poetry is, we try making one. Beginning with an overheard phrase, a misremembered sentence or one stubborn detail from the room, we will see what happens when ordinary language is put under pressure—cut, repeated, broken into lines, made strange. No preparation. No masterpiece required.


Learning outcomes: L01, L03

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 2 Lecture – No ideas but in things: the poetic image

Why speak in abstractions when you can give us a race, a battle, a fish or petals on a wet black bough? Moving from the Imagists to Elizabeth Bishop, Ezra Pound and Bashō, we explore how exact, concrete images make thought visible – and how comparison, concentration and juxtaposition allow a few words to carry far more than they say.


Learning outcomes: L01, L02

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 2 Tutorial – The space between things: haiku

Haiku is often taught as a seventeen-syllable form. More importantly, it is an art of relation: one sharply observed image placed beside another, with the cut between them doing much of the thinking. Reading Japanese haiku in translation alongside English-language examples, we will explore image, juxtaposition and omission before drafting and revising two haiku of our own.


Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 3 Lecture – The pleasures of ulteriority: figures of speech

Language rarely travels in a straight line. Metaphor sees one thing through another; metonymy lets a single detail summon a world; anaphora and chiasmus turn repetition and reversal into rhythm, emphasis and argument. We explore how figures of speech reshape perception, intensify feeling and lodge language in memory – and why some startle while others harden into cliché.


Learning outcomes: L01, L02

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 4 Lecture – Where the line breaks

In prose, the line ends when the page runs out; in poetry, someone makes a choice. We explore how line breaks, enjambment, end-stopping and caesura control pace, emphasis, suspense and double meaning – and what happens when the shape of a poem pulls against its sentences.


Learning outcomes: L01, L02

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 4 Tutorial – The list: a form with an appetite

A list can catalogue, accumulate, argue, boast, mourn or cast a spell. We will gather particulars and shape them through sequence, repetition and variation, discovering how a list becomes a poem – and how its ending can change everything that came before.


Learning outcomes: L03, L04

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 5 Lecture – The measure of a voice: rhythm and sound

A poem happens in time. Its language can hurry, hesitate, circle back or fall silent. We explore how stress, pace, pause, repetition, rhyme and the play of consonants and vowels create movement and expectation – and how rhythm arises not from metre alone, but from the shifting relationship between sentence, line and speaking voice.


Learning outcomes: L01, L02

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 5 Tutorial – A line, repeated, answered: the blues poem

The blues stanza is deceptively simple: a line is spoken, repeated, then answered or turned. We consider the form’s origins in African American musical and oral traditions, explore how repetition produces rhythm, variation and pressure, and write a blues poem of our own. Drafts will be tested aloud and revised for movement, music and surprise.


Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 6 Lecture – The rules make the poem: poetic form

Fourteen lines, nineteen lines, six repeating words: poetic forms make rules, and poets discover what those rules permit. We explore how pattern, repetition and constraint generate expectation; how departures from a pattern acquire meaning; and why inherited forms remain available for reinvention.


Learning outcomes: L01, L02

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 6 Tutorial – Fourteen lines and a turn: the sonnet

A sonnet sets thought in motion, then asks it to change direction. Reading several different uses of the form, we examine how fourteen lines, rhyme, metre and the volta create pressure and possibility. We then draft a sonnet of our own, deciding which conventions to keep, bend or abandon—and what the poem must do to earn its turn.


Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 7 Lecture – The form a poem discovers: free verse

In a sonnet, the form arrives before the poem. In free verse, the poem must discover its form as it goes. We explore how poets create structure through line, sentence, cadence, repetition, image and white space – and how a poem with no inherited pattern decides what belongs, where to turn and when to end.


Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 7 Tutorial – Look again: the object poem

A key, a receipt, a chipped cup: choose something ordinary enough to have become almost invisible. Through sustained attention, we will make the familiar strange, allowing the object’s shape, history and associations to generate a free-verse poem. The challenge is to discover the form this particular object demands.

Preparing for Workshop 1: Your tutor will publish the Group A and Group B roster on Blackboard. All students must upload their first workshop poem by Thursday 10 September at 4pm. Group A poems will be discussed in Week 8 and Group B poems in Week 9.


Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 8 Lecture – Where poems come from: Madeleine Dale on finding inspiration

Inspiration has a reputation for arriving mysteriously and at inconvenient hours. But poets also learn how to court it: by reading, noticing, collecting, misremembering, borrowing forms and following the strange pull of a phrase. Drawing on her own practice, poet Madeleine Dale explores where poems begin—and how to keep writing when inspiration declines to appear.


Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L05

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 8 – Poetry Workshop: Round 1 (Group A)

This week, we begin the workshop sequence at the heart of the second half of the course.

Workshops give your poems sustained attention from a community of readers and can reveal possibilities that are difficult to discover alone. Just as importantly, reading other students’ drafts closely will sharpen your understanding of the choices available in your own writing.

Your tutor will allocate you to Group A or Group B and publish the roster on Blackboard.

As preparation, all students in Groups A and B must have uploaded their first workshop poem of no more than two pages to Blackboard on Thursday 10 September by 4pm. Group A poems will be discussed this week; Group B poems will be discussed next week.

Before the tutorial, print and read each Group A poem closely and more than once. Annotate every poem by hand, identifying its strengths, commenting on particular choices in language, image, sound, line or structure, and noting questions or suggestions that may help the poet revise. Bring the complete set of printed and annotated poems to class and be prepared to refer to particular words and lines. Write your name on each copy. At the end of the workshop, give each annotated poem to its author. Your tutor may review your annotations as evidence of workshop practice.

In the tutorial, we will discuss one draft by each Group A poet. For every poem, we will consider what is most effective, examine how it works, and identify possibilities for its further development.

The tutor will lead the discussion, but a successful workshop depends on the careful preparation and active contribution of every student. The poet listens and takes notes during the discussion, then has an opportunity to respond, ask questions and identify what may be useful for revision.

Everyone attends with the complete set of printed and annotated poems and contributes to the discussion of every poem. Group B poets participate as readers this week; next week, the roles are reversed.

Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 9 Lecture: The poem’s second life: Philip Neilsen on making poems

A published poem conceals the drafts it survived. Drawing on early and final versions of his own work, Philip Neilsen takes us inside the choices, accidents and reversals of revision: the line cut, the stanza moved, the ending discovered late. What can a poet learn from the poem that was not known at the beginning – and how does one decide when to stop?

Learning outcomes: L02, L04, L05

WEEK 9 – Poetry Workshop: Round 1 (Group B)

This week, we turn our attention to the Group B poems. Building on our first workshop, we will deepen our practice as readers: grounding observations in particular words and lines, distinguishing close reading from personal preference, and offering feedback that opens possibilities for revision rather than prescribing solutions.

Before the tutorial, print and read each Group B poem closely and more than once. Annotate every poem, identifying its strengths, commenting on particular choices in language, image, sound, line or structure, and noting questions or possibilities that may help the poet revise. Bring the complete set of printed and annotated poems to class and be prepared to refer to particular words and lines.

In the tutorial, we will discuss one draft by each Group B poet. For every poem, we will consider what is most effective, examine how it works, and identify possibilities for its further development.

The tutor will lead the discussion, but a successful workshop depends on the careful preparation and active contribution of every student. The poet listens and takes notes during the discussion, then has an opportunity to respond, ask questions and identify what may be useful for revision.

Everyone attends with the complete set of printed and annotated poems and contributes to the discussion of every poem. Group A poets now contribute as readers, using what they learned from having their own poems discussed to make their feedback more attentive and useful.

Preparing for the next workshop round: All students must upload their second workshop poem by Thursday 24 September at 4pm. Group B poems will be discussed in Week 10 and Group A poems in Week 11.

Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 10 Lecture – What the picture does not say: ekphrasis

An artwork is already complete, so why write a poem about it? Ekphrasis may begin in description, but it rarely stays there. A poem can enter the scene, invent a missing voice, dispute what the image shows or attend to what lies beyond its frame. Through poems responding to painting, photography and other visual art, we explore what happens when one art form speaks to – and sometimes against – another.

Learning outcomes: L01, L02
learning_activities.topic_title: WEEK 10 Lecture – What the picture does not say: ekphrasis
learning_activities.topic_description: WEEK 10 Lecture – What the picture does not say: ekphrasis An artwork is already complete, so why write a poem about it? Ekphrasis may begin in description, but it rarely stays there. A poem can enter the scene, invent a missing voice, dispute what the image shows or attend to what lies beyond its frame. Through poems responding to painting, photography and other visual art, we explore what happens when one art form speaks to – and sometimes against – another.

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 10 – Poetry Workshop: Round 2 (Group B)

This week, we begin the second workshop round with the Group B poets’ second workshop poems. We will read with increasing precision, offering generous, specific observations and opening a range of possibilities for revision—from individual words and line breaks to larger questions of image, voice, structure and ending. The aim is for each poet to leave with plenty to consider, while retaining the freedom to decide which possibilities serve the poem they want to write.

All students in Groups A and B must have uploaded their second workshop poem — no more than two pages — to Blackboard by Thursday 24 September at 4pm. Group B poems will be discussed this week; Group A poems will be discussed in Week 11.

Before the tutorial, print and read each Group B poem closely and more than once. Annotate every poem, identifying what is particularly effective, examining specific choices in language, image, sound, line or structure, and noting questions or possibilities that may help the poet revise. Bring the complete set of printed and annotated poems to class and be prepared to refer to particular words and lines.

The tutor will lead each discussion. The poet listens and takes notes, then has an opportunity to respond, ask questions and identify what may be useful for revision. Everyone attends with the complete set of printed and annotated poems and contributes to the discussion of every poem.

Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 11 Lecture: The lives of words: diction and the history of English

English is a language of arrivals. Old English words live beside borrowings from Norse, French, Latin and hundreds of other languages, giving poets several ways to name almost anything. We explore how a word’s history, sound, register and associations shape what it can do in a poem. Why does ask feel different from inquire, kingly from royal, house from residence – and how can changing one word alter an entire poem?

Learning outcomes: L01, L02

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 11 – Poetry Workshop: Round 2 (Group A)

This week, we complete the second workshop round with the Group A poets’ second workshop poems. Drawing on what we have learned across the earlier workshops, we will offer each writer close, generous and specific feedback—from individual words, sounds and line breaks to larger questions of image, voice, structure and ending.

All students in Groups A and B must have uploaded their second workshop poem — no more than two pages — to Blackboard by Thursday 24 September at 4pm. Group B poems were discussed in Week 10; Group A poems will be discussed this week.

Before the tutorial, print and read each Group A poem closely and more than once. Annotate every poem, identifying what is particularly effective, examining specific choices in language, image, sound, line or structure, and noting questions or possibilities that may help the poet revise. Bring the complete set of printed and annotated poems to class and be prepared to refer to particular words and lines.

The tutor will lead each discussion. The poet listens and takes notes, then has an opportunity to respond, ask questions and identify what may be useful for revision. Feedback is not a verdict on the poem or a set of instructions to follow. Its purpose is to help the poet see the draft more fully. Each writer must decide which possibilities serve the poem they are trying to make.

Everyone attends with the complete set of printed and annotated poems and contributes to the discussion of every poem. Group B poets return to the role of readers, using their recent experience of receiving feedback to make their responses attentive, generous and useful.

Preparing for Workshop Round 3: All students must upload their third workshop poem — no more than two pages — to Blackboard by 4.00 pm on Thursday 15 October. Group A poems will be discussed in Week 12 and Group B poems in Week 13.

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 12 Lecture – What to keep, what to cut: editing your poetry

Revision can transform a poem’s conception; editing tests every choice it makes. We work through a poem from title to final line, asking where language is vague, predictable or over-explained; whether images, sounds, line breaks and stanzas are doing enough; and what the poem might gain by cutting, compressing or rearranging. How do you become a rigorous reader of your own work without editing away what made it alive?

Learning outcomes: L02, L04

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 12 – Poetry Workshop: Round 3 (Group A)

This week, we begin our third and final workshop round with new poems from the Group A poets. By now, we have developed a shared language for discussing drafts and become more confident in grounding our responses in particular words, sounds and lines. This final round is an opportunity to bring that experience together as both poets and readers.

All students in Groups A and B must have uploaded their third workshop poem — no more than two pages — to Blackboard by 4.00 pm on Thursday 15 October. Group A poems will be discussed this week; Group B poems will be discussed in Week 13.

Before the tutorial, print, read and annotate each Group A poem. Bring the complete set to class and be prepared to refer to particular words and lines.

In the tutorial, we will identify what is already effective and explore possibilities for revision. The aim is not to produce as many suggestions as possible, but to help each poet recognise the revisions that matter most.

Everyone attends and contributes to the discussion of every poem. As the final portfolio approaches, use what you learn from these discussions to reconsider the possibilities within your own work.

Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 13 Lecture – After the poem is written: finding its readers

Finishing a poem is not the same as finding it a life. We map the contemporary poetry world: magazines, publishers, prizes, readings, festivals, residencies and retreats—and consider how poets find the right home for their work. What do editors look for? Which opportunities genuinely sustain a writing life, and which merely sell writers the hope of one?

Learning outcomes: L04, L05

learning_activities.topic:
WEEK 13 – Poetry Workshop: Round 3 (Group B)

This week, we complete our final workshop round with new poems from the Group B poets. Drawing on the reading and discussion we have practised throughout the semester, we will give each draft close, generous and specific attention. We will identify what is already effective and explore possibilities for revision—from particular words, images, sounds and line breaks to larger questions of voice, movement, structure and ending. Each poet remains free to accept, adapt or set aside any suggestion.

All students must have uploaded their third workshop poem — no more than two pages — to Blackboard by Thursday 15 October at 4pm. Group A poems were discussed last week; Group B poems will be discussed this week.

Before the tutorial, print, read and annotate each Group B poem. Bring the complete set to class and be prepared to refer to particular words and lines.

Everyone attends and contributes to the discussion of every poem. This final workshop marks the transition from collaborative drafting to the independent decisions through which your final portfolio will take shape.

If you have found the workshops useful, you may wish to continue exchanging poems with classmates during revision week. Any such exchange is voluntary: agree on the kind of response that would be most helpful, treat one another’s drafts as confidential, and remember that each writer remains responsible for the final poem.

Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04
